body.text: Liberal preferences could determine key inner-Melbourne seats at Victorian election

With Victorian Labor's vote apparently set to sink to record lows, and a growing appetite among voters for minor parties and independents, it stands to reason that the Greens should be hopeful of making some gains in the state parliament in this month's election.

Support for the Greens hasn't surged to anywhere near the levels experienced by One Nation in the state, but polls do suggest the party has a chance to make a modest improvement on where it has been stuck for more than 20 years.

One poll this month put the party at 17 per cent statewide, just one point below Labor, but that has been an outlier. Most polls released in the last couple of months peg the party closer to 14 or 15 per cent, which would still represent a noteworthy lift.
If that increase in statewide vote bears out on election night, and is concentrated in the right places, it could help the party paint more of inner-Melbourne's electoral map green.
An unpopular Labor government makes it easier for the minor party to convert progressives to their cause, and the party is hoping to gain a handful of seats at the end of the month.
But Ellen Sandell's party has to overcome a setback along the way: Liberal preferences.
Greens hopes in Melbourne's inner electorates
The Greens have been able to turn a relatively modest statewide primary into seats in the lower house by virtue of the fact that its vote is concentrated in the inner suburbs.
The party gets less than 10 per cent of the vote in most districts, but in 2022, it got at least a third of the primary vote in four (and won them all).
Those seats, and nearly all of the next highest dozen, are in the suburbs closest to Melbourne's CBD, especially in the inner north.

Aside from retaining their current seats of Brunswick, Melbourne, and Richmond, the party wants to win back Prahran which it lost in a by-election in 2025. It also hopes to gain seats like Northcote, Pascoe Vale, Preston and Footscray from Labor, where its candidates fell narrowly short of wins in 2022.
The Greens very efficient vote in the inner suburbs may help them win a record seat haul this year. But beyond those seats, its gains get trickier.

The party also polls relatively well in Albert Park, Ivanhoe, and Oakleigh, but the party needs to overtake Labor to make it into the final two in those seats. In 2022, Greens candidates ran at least 15 percentage points behind Labor in all three.
At the federal level new Greens leader David Shoebridge has declared his party's goal is to replace the Labor Party, and that language has been echoed by Victorian leader Ellen Sandell.
In order replace Labor, it would need to be growing its vote in other areas as well, and the Liberals appear to be trying to block that from happening.
Liberal preferences may determine winners in the inner suburbs
In the seats it wants to gain for the first time, the Greens main competition is Labor, meaning the preferences of Liberal voters will likely determine the winner.
Four years ago, most Liberal voters preferenced Greens candidates above Labor in these seats, at the suggestion of the party's how-to-vote cards.
This time, the opposition has cruelled the Greens chances of making a breakthrough, by issuing how-to-vote cards with Labor on top in all of these seats bar Brunswick and Footscray.
This is consistent with the Liberals approach at the federal level, where Greens have been put behind Labor since the 2013 election.
The Victorian Liberals have done the same, except for in 2022.

Preference recommendations are often more about the political theatre than the impact they have at the ballot box. However, Liberal voters are some of the most likely to follow how to vote recommendations.

That's why the Liberals' decision in these seats, where the party is likely to come third, is the single most impactful preference recommendation in the state election. All others pale in significance.
We can see it in election results data because we have a natural experiment: the Liberal Party has now flip-flopped back and forth on its how-to-vote cards in inner Melbourne.

In 2022, when the Liberal candidate was excluded in Pascoe Vale and Northcote, more than 60 per cent of the votes that were distributed went to the Greens over Labor (excluding votes that went to someone else).
In 2018, when the party recommended Labor over the Greens, Liberal flows to the minor party were 20-25 percentage points lower.
That is to say, which of Labor or the Greens the Liberals put last determines where up to a quarter of their preferences go.
That's equivalent to the final margins in the seat shifting by between two and five percentage points in favour of Labor, based on last election's figures.
In Prahran, Labor has issued an 'open ticket', so preference flows to The Greens there may also be weaker than 2022.
To win, The Greens need to see their vote increase by enough to overcome both the margin in the seats and the weaker flows they should expect from major party voters.

It may not matter all that much in the end, if the Greens primary vote grows substantially. For example, the party barely lost in Northcote four years ago, and its candidate Campbell Gome is making a second tilt at the seat in an environment where the Greens appear to be up and Labor is down.

But the opposition, which appears increasingly likely to be in a position to form government at the end of the month, has decided not to make it easy for them, and it is a blow for the party's larger aspirations.
There is a chance that it helps Labor hold on to some of its furniture, even if the rest of its house is on fire.
